title: Mira Nair's Diwali Dinner in New York Doubles as Writers' Fundraiser
excerpt: Authors, filmmakers and artists gathered at Indian restaurant Passerine for a Diwali dinner that raised funds for the Asian American Writers' Workshop and turned, warmly, to India's youth protests.
body:
• Filmmaker Mira Nair hosted an intimate Diwali dinner at Passerine in New York this week, gathering authors, filmmakers, artists and writers, according to The New York Times.
  • The evening doubled as a fundraising dinner for the Asian American Writers' Workshop, an eyewitness account by writer Amitava Kumar confirms.
  • Guests including Salman Rushdie voiced support for India's bubbling youth democracy movement, turning a festival meal into a conversation about India itself.
  • For diaspora readers, the dinner is a model Diwali gathering: a good Indian restaurant table, a cause worth supporting, and a birthday cake for the host, whose birthday fell on October 15.

Authors, filmmakers, artists and writers gathered at the New York restaurant Passerine this week for an intimate Diwali dinner hosted by filmmaker Mira Nair, according to The New York Times. The dinner celebrated Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, in a city where the festival has become a fixture of the autumn cultural calendar for South Asian New Yorkers and their friends.

The gathering was more than a party. Writer Amitava Kumar, who attended as a guest, described the evening in a first-person account as a fundraising dinner for the Asian American Writers' Workshop, held in the run-up to Diwali. Read his account here. That dual purpose — festival celebration and literary fundraising — shaped the conversation around the table.

A Dinner That Turned to India

Several guests voiced support for what the Times called the bubbling youth democracy movement in India. Kumar reported that Salman Rushdie told the room that something was happening in India and that young people there had given older observers a hopeful moment. Rushdie also recalled growing up in Bombay, where, in his telling, festivals belonged to everyone — Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians and Parsis celebrated together — and suggested that shared spirit felt alive in the room that night, even if it felt less certain in India itself.

"a cockroach mom"

— Mira Nair, on her pride in India's young protesters, as reported by a guest at the dinner

Nair herself, according to Kumar, said she was proud of the young Indians protesting for democracy and jokingly described herself in those terms. The exchange gave the evening its headline moment: a Diwali table in Manhattan talking, with affection and worry in equal measure, about street protests thousands of miles away.

Food at the Centre

The setting mattered. Passerine is an Indian restaurant, and the meal was led by its chef, Gaurav Bathla, who, Kumar reported, produced a birthday cake for Nair, whose birthday fell on October 15. A Diwali dinner in a serious Indian dining room makes a point that diaspora hosts understand well: the food is not decoration. Regional Indian cooking, served properly, carries the festival for guests who may know Diwali only as a date in the calendar.

That is why dinners like this one travel well as a template. A restaurant table removes the burden of cooking for twenty, keeps the menu unmistakably Indian, and lets the host do what Nair did — gather writers, artists and filmmakers and let conversation carry the night. Kumar's account places former Vanity Fair editor Radhika Jones among the guests who brought him along, underlining the literary character of the room.

Why It Resonates in the Diaspora

For Indian Americans, Diwali dinners have become a public language. They signal that a festival once celebrated mainly at home and in temples now sits comfortably in New York's restaurant and fundraising life, without losing its meaning of light over darkness. Nair, whose films have long moved between India and its diaspora, is a natural host for that translation.

The political turn in the conversation also reflects a wider diaspora reality in 2026: celebrations of India abroad increasingly include debate about India. Pride, criticism and homesickness shared the same table at Passerine, according to both accounts of the night.

What to Watch

Diwali events continue across New York through the festival period, from temple celebrations to restaurant dinners and literary fundraisers. Readers planning their own gathering can take the Passerine lesson directly: book an Indian restaurant early, anchor the evening in a cause or a conversation, and let the food do the cultural work it has always done at Diwali.
